reference.source: Clinical genetics and paediatric endocrinology references
clinicalPearls: Rare autosomal dominant dysplasia caused by activating (constitutively active) mutations of PTH1R, the receptor shared by parathyroid hormone and PTH-related peptide.
The mutant receptor signals independently of its ligands, producing a biochemical picture of parathyroid hormone excess despite low or undetectable circulating PTH and PTHrP.
Severe short-limbed short stature with characteristic facies (frontal bossing, hypertelorism, micrognathia) and a flexed, crouching stance.
Radiographs show gross metaphyseal cupping, fraying and expansion that can closely resemble severe rickets.
Biochemistry shows hypercalcaemia with hypophosphataemia and suppressed PTH — the mirror image of most rickets.
Chronic hypercalcaemia and hypercalciuria predispose to nephrocalcinosis and progressive renal impairment.
With age the metaphyseal lesions may appear cyst-like and later calcify, while limb deformity and disability remain marked.
Most cases are sporadic and arise from de novo mutations, so a negative family history does not exclude the diagnosis.
reference.pathophysiology: The disorder results from heterozygous activating mutations in PTH1R (PTHR1), which encodes the class B G-protein-coupled receptor for both parathyroid hormone and PTH-related peptide. Mutations affecting the transmembrane helices (such as the classic His223Arg, Thr410Pro and Ile458Arg substitutions) lock the receptor in a ligand-independent, constitutively active state that drives tonic Gs–cAMP signalling. In the growth plate, PTHrP acting through PTH1R normally keeps chondrocytes proliferating and delays their hypertrophic differentiation; constitutive activation exaggerates and disorganises this signal, delaying hypertrophic differentiation and mineralisation and producing the severe metaphyseal chondrodysplasia. In bone and the renal proximal tubule the same unregulated signalling mimics chronic parathyroid hormone excess, giving hypercalcaemia, hypophosphataemia and increased bone turnover even though endogenous PTH and PTHrP are appropriately suppressed. Inheritance is autosomal dominant, and most cases are de novo.
additionalDifferentials: Severe rickets, whether nutritional or hereditary hypophosphataemic
Other causes of infantile hypercalcaemia (Williams syndrome, subcutaneous fat necrosis, hypervitaminosis D)
Primary or neonatal severe hyperparathyroidism related to the calcium-sensing receptor
Other metaphyseal dysplasias such as the McKusick and Spahr types
additionalInvestigations: Skeletal survey demonstrating severe metaphyseal cupping and fraying
Corrected or ionised calcium, phosphate and magnesium
Parathyroid hormone and, where available, PTHrP (both typically low or undetectable)
Urine calcium-to-creatinine ratio and renal ultrasound to detect nephrocalcinosis
Alkaline phosphatase and vitamin D metabolites to help exclude rickets
redFlags: Symptomatic hypercalcaemia with dehydration, vomiting, lethargy or polyuria
Failure to thrive or feeding difficulty in infancy
Airway or feeding compromise from craniofacial involvement
reference.prognosis: The outlook is guarded, with lifelong severe short stature and skeletal deformity and a risk of nephrocalcinosis and renal impairment from chronic hypercalcaemia. Hypercalcaemia often becomes less marked in adulthood, but the deformity and disability persist.
pitfalls: Diagnosing rickets from the radiographs and giving vitamin D, which can aggravate the hypercalcaemia.
Assuming that hypercalcaemia must mean a raised parathyroid hormone, when in Jansen disease PTH is suppressed.
Missing nephrocalcinosis because renal imaging and urinary calcium were not checked.
Discounting the diagnosis in a sporadic case simply because there is no family history.
